```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
# move2utils is a suggested package, available from GitHub, which is needed
# by some of the chunks
has_move2utils <- requireNamespace("move2utils", quietly = TRUE)
```

Data from tracking devices are rarely ready for analysis. Loggers may fail to
get a fix and record a dummy location instead, the same record may be
downloaded twice, some locations may be far from the true position of the
animal, and the interval between fixes may vary. This article shows how to read
tracking data into a tibble of tracks, and how to find and fix these problems,
one step at a time, inspecting the data after each step.

We use the Antarctic shag tracks from the main vignette
(`vignette("tidytracks")`), to which we added some of the errors that are
typical of raw tracking data. Remember that these data were modified to show
the functionality of `tidytracks`, and should not be used for analyses of shag
movement. All the files used in this article are in the directory
`vignettes/articles/data` of the source code of the package.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(tidytracks)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
```

# Reading data

`tt_read_data()` reads a table of events from a CSV file (or from a
`data.frame`). The table must have a column identifying the track of each
event, two columns with the coordinates, and the date-time of each event,
either in a single column or in separate date and time columns (see the main
vignette for more details).

## Date-time formats

Date-times are stored in many different formats. If `format_date_time` is not
given, `tt_read_data()` tries a set of common formats: dates as
year-month-day, day/month/year or month/day/year (with `/` or `-` as
separators), followed by the time as hours:minutes:seconds or hours:minutes. To
see how this works, we use three small files with the first five locations of
bird `kb_17`, each with its date-times in a different format.

### Separate date and time columns

In the first file, the date (as day/month/year) and the time are in separate
columns:

```{r read_dmy_csv}
read.csv("data/shags_dates_dmy.csv")
```

We give both columns to `col_date_time`, and they are combined into a single
`date_time` column:

```{r read_dmy}
shags_dmy <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/shags_dates_dmy.csv",
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = c("date", "time")
)
```

```{r time_dmy}
event_time(shags_dmy)
```

The format was detected correctly. Note that, by default, date-times are
assumed to be in UTC (`time_zone = "UTC"`), and coordinates to be longitude and
latitude on WGS 84 (`crs = 4326`).

### Month/day/year dates

In the second file, the dates are given as month/day/year:

```{r read_mdy_csv}
read.csv("data/shags_dates_mdy.csv")
```

These dates are ambiguous: `01/04/2022` could be the 4th of January or the 1st
of April. Day/month/year formats are tried before month/day/year formats, so
the dates are read as the 1st of April, without any warning:

```{r read_mdy_auto}
shags_mdy <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/shags_dates_mdy.csv",
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time"
)
```

```{r time_mdy_auto}
event_time(shags_mdy)
```

Month/day/year would be detected if any of the days was after the 12th (e.g.
`01/13/2022`), as that cannot be read as day/month/year. To avoid any
ambiguity, we give the format with `format_date_time`, using the codes of
`strptime()`: `%m` for the month, `%d` for the day, `%Y` for the year (with the
century), and `%H`, `%M` and `%S` for hours, minutes and seconds:

```{r read_mdy_format}
shags_mdy <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/shags_dates_mdy.csv",
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time",
  format_date_time = "%m/%d/%Y %H:%M:%S"
)
```

```{r time_mdy_format}
event_time(shags_mdy)
```

### ISO 8601 date-times

Many devices and online databases use the ISO 8601 standard, with a `T` between
the date and the time, and a `Z` at the end for UTC:

```{r read_iso_csv}
read.csv("data/shags_dates_iso.csv")
```

This format is not among those detected automatically, so `tt_read_data()`
gives an error:

```{r read_iso_auto, error = TRUE}
shags_iso <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/shags_dates_iso.csv",
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time"
)
```

We can read it by giving the format, with `T` and `Z` as literal characters:

```{r read_iso_format}
shags_iso <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/shags_dates_iso.csv",
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time",
  format_date_time = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"
)
```

```{r time_iso}
event_time(shags_iso)
```

If the date-times were recorded in local time rather than UTC, give their time
zone with `time_zone` (e.g. `time_zone = "Antarctica/Rothera"`; see
`OlsonNames()` for the names of all time zones).

## The example dataset

The file `shags_raw.csv` has the tracks of the 9 shags of the main vignette, in
the state in which they could come from the loggers. Its date-times are in the
year-month-day format, which is detected automatically:

```{r read_raw}
shags_tt <- tt_read_data(
  events = "data/shags_raw.csv",
  col_track_id = "bird_id",
  col_coords = c("lon", "lat"),
  col_date_time = "date_time",
  time_zone = "UTC",
  crs = 4326
)
```

Many of the functions used below require the events to be ordered by time
within each track, so we start by ordering them:

```{r order_raw}
shags_tt <- shags_tt %>% tt_order_time()
```

```{r inspect_raw}
shags_tt
```

# Inspecting the raw data

Let us plot the locations of all the events:

```{r plot_raw, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_point(data = shags_tt, aes(colour = bird_id))
```

All the birds were tracked from a colony in Antarctica, but some events are on
the equator, at 0° longitude and 0° latitude: a point known as "null island".
Some loggers record a location of (0, 0) when they fail to get a fix, and
missing coordinates can also be turned into zeros when data are processed.

`track_summary_health()` gives an overview of the sampling of each track:

```{r health_raw}
track_summary_health(shags_tt)
```

For each track, we get the median interval between events and the duration of
the track (both in seconds), the number of events expected given that interval
and duration, the actual number of events, and the proportion of the expected
events that are missing. Most birds were tracked every 2 minutes, but four of
them (`kb_17`, `kb_19`, `kb_27` and `kb_29`) were tracked every 10 minutes.

# Removing locations at null island

We find the events at null island from their coordinates:

```{r null_island}
# the coordinates (longitude and latitude) of each event
coords <- st_coordinates(shags_tt)
# the events at null island
at_null_island <- coords[, "X"] == 0 & coords[, "Y"] == 0
sum(at_null_island)
```

and remove them:

```{r remove_null_island}
shags_tt <- shags_tt %>% filter(!at_null_island)
```

To plot the locations around the colony, we use the azimuthal equidistant
projection centred on the colony from the main vignette:

```{r projection}
shags_crs <- paste0(
  "+proj=aeqd +lon_0=-68 +lat_0=-67 ",
  "+units=m +datum=WGS84 +no_defs"
)
```

```{r plot_no_null_island, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_point(data = shags_tt, aes(colour = bird_id)) +
  coord_sf(crs = shags_crs) +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

All the locations are now around the colony. The failed fixes left gaps in the
tracks:

```{r health_no_null_island}
track_summary_health(shags_tt)
```

The proportion of missing events has increased for most tracks, in
particular for `kb_43`, which now has a long gap (we will come back to it when
resampling the tracks).

# Removing duplicated records

Some records may be duplicated, for example if the data were downloaded twice
from a logger. Many methods require each track to have at most one location
per time stamp, which we can check with
`mt_has_unique_location_time_records()` from `move2` (which is loaded with
`tidytracks`):

```{r check_duplicates}
mt_has_unique_location_time_records(shags_tt)
```

There are duplicated time stamps. `mt_unique()` flags the records that are
copies of other records (`FALSE`), so we can count them:

```{r count_duplicates}
sum(!mt_unique(shags_tt))
```

and `mt_filter_unique()` removes them:

```{r remove_duplicates}
shags_tt <- shags_tt %>% mt_filter_unique()
```

```{r check_no_duplicates}
mt_has_unique_location_time_records(shags_tt)
```

By default, `mt_filter_unique()` only removes the records that are identical
to (or a subset of) another record with the same time stamp. In these data,
some of the duplicated time stamps had a second record at null island, which
we have already removed, so all the remaining duplicates were exact copies.
When records with the same time stamp differ (e.g. in their location),
`mt_filter_unique()` keeps them all and gives a warning: we then have to decide
which record to keep (see the `criterion` argument of `mt_filter_unique()`).

```{r health_no_duplicates}
track_summary_health(shags_tt)
```

The tracks that had duplicated records now have fewer events.

# Removing outliers

## Speeds

Locations that are far from the true position of the animal result in
unrealistic speeds. Let us compute the speed of each step (in km/h):

```{r speed}
shags_tt <- shags_tt %>%
  mutate(speed = event_speed(., units = as_units("km/h")))
```

```{r summary_speed}
summary(shags_tt$speed)
```

and plot it along the tracks:

```{r plot_speed, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_path(data = shags_tt, aes(colour = speed)) +
  facet_wrap(~bird_id) +
  coord_sf(crs = shags_crs) +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

Some steps are far faster than a shag can fly (shags have been observed flying
at 58 km/h, see the main vignette).

## Choosing a maximum speed

Speed filters need a maximum speed. When no published value is available for a
species, `max_speed_allometric()` predicts the maximum speed of an animal from
its body mass and mode of locomotion (Hirt et al. 2017). For a flying bird of
about 2.5 kg:

```{r allometric, eval = has_move2utils}
# the prediction is in m/s; convert it to km/h to compare with published values
max_speed_allometric(as_units(2.5, "kg"), mode = "flying") %>%
  set_units("km/h")
```

This is a ceiling on what an animal of that mass can physically do, and a
published, species-specific value should be preferred when available.

Alternatively, `track_suggest_max_speed()` looks, in each track, for a break
in the distribution of speeds that separates plausible steps from outliers:

```{r suggest_speed, eval = has_move2utils}
# one suggestion per track (NA if no break is found)
track_suggest_max_speed(shags_tt, units = as_units("km/h"))
```

Data-driven suggestions must always be checked against the biology of the
species: for example, for `kb_38`, which hardly moved, a break is more likely
to separate resting from moving than plausible steps from outliers. Here, we
use the maximum speed of 60 km/h from the main vignette.

These two functions, as well as `event_flag_outliers()` and
`tt_clean_outliers()` below, require the suggested package `move2utils` (see
the article "Using move2utils with tidytracks").

## Comparing methods to detect outliers

`event_flag_mcconnell()` flags outliers with McConnell's filter (McConnell et
al. 1992), and `event_flag_outliers()` with one of the methods of `move2utils`
(described by Safi 2026), both returning `TRUE` for valid events. Let us compare
McConnell's filter with three of these methods: a hard speed cap at the same
maximum speed, the detour method (which flags out-and-back spikes) and
`mt_clean_track()`, the default, which combines several methods and chooses its
thresholds from the data:

```{r outliers, eval = has_move2utils}
shags_flags <- shags_tt %>%
  mutate(
    # McConnell's filter
    mcconnell = event_flag_mcconnell(., max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h")),
    # a fixed speed cap at the same speed, rather than one chosen from the data
    speed_cap = event_flag_outliers(
      .,
      method = "speed_cap",
      v_max = as_units(60, "km/h"),
      threshold_type = "hard"
    ),
    # ignore spikes with legs shorter than 100 m, to avoid flagging GPS jitter
    # while the birds rest
    detour = event_flag_outliers(
      .,
      method = "detour",
      min_leg = as_units(100, "m")
    ),
    # the default method, with all thresholds chosen from the data
    clean_track = event_flag_outliers(.)
  )
```

```{r count_outliers, eval = has_move2utils}
# count the events flagged (FALSE) by each method
shags_flags %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  summarise(across(c(mcconnell, speed_cap, detour, clean_track), ~ sum(!.x)))
```

The methods flag very different numbers of events. Let us look at where they
are, for three of the birds:

```{r outliers_long, eval = has_move2utils}
shags_flags_long <- shags_flags %>%
  filter(bird_id %in% c("kb_19", "kb_27", "kb_42")) %>%
  # project the locations, so that distances are not distorted
  st_transform(shags_crs) %>%
  mutate(
    x = st_coordinates(.)[, 1],
    y = st_coordinates(.)[, 2]
  ) %>%
  as.data.frame(drop_geometry = TRUE) %>%
  # one row per event and method, to plot the methods in separate panels
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    c(mcconnell, speed_cap, detour, clean_track),
    names_to = "method",
    values_to = "valid"
  )
```

```{r plot_outliers, eval = has_move2utils, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 8}
ggplot(shags_flags_long, aes(x, y)) +
  geom_path(colour = "grey60") +
  # flagged events in red
  geom_point(
    data = filter(shags_flags_long, !valid),
    colour = "red",
    size = 0.8
  ) +
  facet_grid(method ~ bird_id, scales = "free") +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

The speed cap flags the events at both ends of every step faster than 60 km/h,
whilst McConnell's filter, which uses the speeds to the neighbouring events,
flags a single event per spike, and keeps steps that are only just too fast.
With its default settings, `mt_clean_track()` can also flag events where the
birds were moving slowly. Whatever the method, look at the flagged events
before removing them. To inspect the diagnostics of a `move2utils` method, call
it directly on the tibble of tracks, e.g.
`move2utils::mt_clean_track(shags_tt, remove = FALSE)`.

## Removing outliers with McConnell's filter

We remove the outliers with McConnell's filter, as in the main vignette:

```{r mcconnell}
shags_clean <- shags_tt %>%
  tt_clean_mcconnell(max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h"))
```

```{r mcconnell_n}
# the number of events removed
nrow(shags_tt) - nrow(shags_clean)
```

`tt_clean_outliers()` removes outliers in the same way with the methods of
`move2utils`, e.g. `tt_clean_outliers(shags_tt, method = "detour")`.

We recompute the speeds, as removing events changes the steps:

```{r speed_clean}
shags_clean <- shags_clean %>%
  mutate(speed = event_speed(., units = as_units("km/h")))
```

```{r summary_speed_clean}
summary(shags_clean$speed)
```

```{r plot_speed_clean, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_path(data = shags_clean, aes(colour = speed)) +
  facet_wrap(~bird_id) +
  coord_sf(crs = shags_crs) +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

The spikes with unrealistic speeds have gone. Note that McConnell's filter
uses the speeds to the previous and next events, so it can keep a step that is
just above the maximum speed, and can miss one of two consecutive outliers;
recomputing the speeds and running the filter again would remove the latter.

```{r health_clean}
track_summary_health(shags_clean)
```

# Interpolating missing locations

Removing outliers leaves gaps in the tracks. Alternatively, we can keep the
time stamps of the outliers, and move them to a location interpolated between
the previous and the next valid locations. To see which events are moved, we
first flag the outliers:

```{r flag_outliers}
shags_flagged <- shags_tt %>%
  mutate(outlier = !event_flag_mcconnell(., max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h")))
```

and then interpolate their locations with `flag_action = "interpolate"`:

```{r interpolate}
shags_interpolated <- shags_flagged %>%
  tt_clean_mcconnell(
    max_speed = as_units(60, "km/h"),
    flag_action = "interpolate"
  )
```

No event was removed:

```{r interpolate_n}
nrow(shags_interpolated) == nrow(shags_tt)
```

Plotting the interpolated events in red:

```{r plot_interpolated, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_path(data = shags_interpolated, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_interpolated, outlier),
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~bird_id) +
  coord_sf(crs = shags_crs) +
  theme(
    aspect.ratio = 1,
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

`tt_clean_outliers()` interpolates outliers in the same way:

```{r clean_outliers, eval = has_move2utils}
shags_interpolated_cap <- shags_tt %>%
  tt_clean_outliers(
    method = "speed_cap",
    v_max = as_units(60, "km/h"),
    threshold_type = "hard",
    # move the outliers to an interpolated location, rather than removing them
    flag_action = "interpolate"
  )
```

With `flag_action = "null"`, both functions keep the time stamps of the
outliers but leave them without a location, which can be interpolated later
with `move2::mt_interpolate()`.

# Resampling tracks to a regular interval

After cleaning, the intervals between events are irregular:

```{r intervals}
summary(event_interval(shags_clean, units = as_units("min")))
```

Most intervals are about 2 or 10 minutes, the two sampling schedules of the
loggers, but the failed fixes and the outliers that we removed left longer
intervals, and some tracks have gaps of several hours (the `NA`s are the last
event of each track). Many analyses need regular tracks, with the same
interval between all events. `tt_regular_time()` resamples each track at a
regular interval, interpolating the locations along the track. Let us resample
all the tracks every 10 minutes:

```{r regular}
shags_regular <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_regular_time(interval = as_units(10, "min"))
```

```{r health_regular}
track_summary_health(shags_regular)
```

All tracks now have an event every 10 minutes (600 seconds), and no missing
events. Let us compare the original (black) and resampled (red) events of
`kb_43`:

```{r plot_regular, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_clean, bird_id == "kb_43"),
    size = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_regular, bird_id == "kb_43"),
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  coord_sf(crs = shags_crs) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The resampled events follow the track, but they also fill, with a straight
line, the gap of about 1.5 hours left by the failed fixes of `kb_43`. A
straight line is a reasonable guess for short gaps, but the longer the gap,
the less likely it is to be the path that the bird took. `max_time_lag` sets
the longest gap to interpolate over; no events are created in longer gaps:

```{r regular_max_lag}
shags_regular <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_regular_time(
    interval = as_units(10, "min"),
    max_time_lag = as_units(1, "h")
  )
```

```{r plot_regular_max_lag, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3}
ggplot() +
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_clean, bird_id == "kb_43"),
    size = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_event_point(
    data = filter(shags_regular, bird_id == "kb_43"),
    colour = "red"
  ) +
  coord_sf(crs = shags_crs) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

```{r health_regular_max_lag}
track_summary_health(shags_regular)
```

The gaps longer than one hour are now missing events again. Each track is
resampled from its first event, so the time stamps of different tracks do not
match; with `snap_times = TRUE`, all tracks are resampled at whole multiples
of the interval (e.g. at 10:00, 10:10, 10:20...), so that tracks recorded at
the same time share their time stamps.

## Thinning tracks

`tt_regular_time()` creates new locations by interpolation. To keep the
original locations instead, `tt_thin_time()` keeps the largest subset of
events whose intervals are within a tolerance of the target interval (by
default, a tenth of it). It requires the suggested package `move2utils`. We
thin all the tracks to 10 minutes:

```{r thin_time, eval = has_move2utils}
# keep events 10 minutes apart (9 to 11 minutes, with the default tolerance)
shags_10min <- shags_clean %>%
  tt_thin_time(interval = as_units(10, "min"))
```

```{r thin_time_intervals, eval = has_move2utils}
# the intervals between the events kept
summary(event_interval(shags_10min, units = as_units("min")))
```

The longer intervals are gaps in the data, which thinning never bridges.
`tt_thin_distance()` similarly thins tracks by the distance travelled along
them (see the article "Using move2utils with tidytracks").

# Summary

A typical workflow to read and clean tracking data is:

1. read the data with `tt_read_data()`, checking that the date-times have been
   parsed correctly (and giving `format_date_time` if needed);
2. order the events by time within each track with `tt_order_time()`;
3. remove the locations at null island (and any other impossible locations);
4. remove duplicated records with `mt_filter_unique()`;
5. remove, or interpolate, outliers with `tt_clean_mcconnell()` or
   `tt_clean_outliers()`;
6. if needed, resample the tracks at a regular interval with
   `tt_regular_time()`, or thin them with `tt_thin_time()`.

After each step, plots and `track_summary_health()` help to check what has
changed.

# References

Hirt, M. R., Jetz, W., Rall, B. C. & Brose, U. (2017). A general scaling law
reveals why the largest animals are not the fastest. *Nature Ecology &
Evolution*, 1, 1116-1122.

McConnell, B. J., Chambers, C. & Fedak, M. A. (1992). Foraging ecology of
southern elephant seals in relation to the bathymetry and productivity of the
Southern Ocean. *Antarctic Science*, 4, 393-398.

Safi, K. (2026). Self-thresholding hierarchical outlier-detection for animal
movement tracks. *bioRxiv*. <https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.11.737894>
